content.body:
The 2026 WTA 1000 season is in the books, with nine players crowned champions across 10 tournaments.

Four of those lifted a WTA 1000 trophy for the first time; five added to existing hauls at this level. From injury comebacks to surges in form, from home-soil glory to historic feats, each title run marked a riveting chapter in the WTA's year. But which was your favorite? Rewind through the champions' best points, then have your say below.

1. Karolina Muchova, Doha

R1: d. Jaqueline Cristian 6-2, 6-3
R2: d. [Q] Tereza Valentova 6-1, 6-4
R3: d. Karolina Pliskova 5-2, ret.
QF: d. Anna Kalinskaya 6-3, 6-4
SF: d. Maria Sakkari 3-6, 6-4, 6-1
F: d. [10] Victoria Mboko 6-4, 7-5

No. 14 seed Muchova snapped a title drought stretching back over six years to lift her second career trophy (following Seoul 2019), and the first at WTA 1000 level, at the Qatar TotalEnergies Open. It foreshadowed a career-best season for the Czech that's also included a second Grand Slam final appearance at Wimbledon and a third title in Bad Homburg. Muchova's defeat of Victoria Mboko in the final was the third of six Top 10 wins she has scored so far in 2026 -- her highest number in a single season.

2. Jessica Pegula, Dubai

R1: bye
R2: d. [Q] Varvara Gracheva 6-4, 6-0
R3: d. [16] Iva Jovic 6-4, 6-2
QF: d. [12] Clara Tauson 6-3, 2-6, 6-4
SF: d. [2] Amanda Anisimova 1-6, 6-4, 6-3
F: d. [7] Elina Svitolina 6-2, 6-4

No. 4 seed Pegula won her fourth career WTA 1000 tournament at the Dubai Duty Free Tennis Championships, and her 10th title overall. The American claimed two of her seven Top 10 wins of 2026 so far en route to the trophy, including a comeback from 6-1, 2-0 down in the semifinals against Amanda Anisimova.

3. Aryna Sabalenka, Indian Wells

R1: bye
R2: d. [Q] Himeno Sakatsume 6-4, 6-2
R3: d. Jaqueline Cristian 6-4, 6-1
R4: d. [16] Naomi Osaka 6-2, 6-4
QF: d. [10] Victoria Mboko 7-6(0), 6-4
SF: d. [14] Linda Noskova 6-3, 6-4
F: d. [3] Elena Rybakina 3-6, 6-3, 7-6(6)

After two previous losses in the BNP Paribas Open final in 2023 and 2025, No. 1 seed Sabalenka claimed her first Indian Wells title after saving one championship point in the final against Elena Rybakina -- avenging her loss to the Kazakhstani player in the Australian Open final. Sabalenka scored two of her seven Top 10 wins of 2026 so far en route to the trophy.

4. Aryna Sabalenka, Miami

R1: bye
R2: d. Ann Li 7-6(5), 6-4
R3: d. Caty McNally 6-4, 6-2
R4: d. [23] Zheng Qinwen 6-3, 6-4
QF: d. Hailey Baptiste 6-4, 6-4
SF: d. [3] Elena Rybakina 6-4, 6-3
F: d. [4] Coco Gauff 6-2, 4-6, 6-3

No. 1 seed Sabalenka became the fifth woman in the Open Era to successfully complete the Sunshine Double after following her Indian Wells title by defending her Miami Open crown. She notched another pair of Top 10 wins along the way, and the two consecutive trophies spearheaded her third career-best 15-match winning streak.

5. Marta Kostyuk, Madrid

R1: bye
R2: d. Yulia Putintseva 6-1, 6-3
R3: d. [5] Jessica Pegula 6-1, 6-4
R4: d. Caty McNally 6-2, 6-3
QF: d. [13] Linda Noskova 7-6(1), 6-0
SF: d. [LL] Anastasia Potapova 6-2, 1-6, 6-1
F: d. [9] Mirra Andreeva 6-3, 7-5

No. 26 seed Kostyuk compiled a 17-match clay-court winning streak, the longest at tour level this year, that included her first career WTA 1000 trophy at the Mutua Madrid Open. It also enabled the Ukrainian, who began the season at No. 26, to make her Top 10 debut in September. Kostyuk notched two of her eight Top 10 wins of 2026 so far in Madrid.

6. Elina Svitolina, Rome

R1: bye
R2: d. [Q] Noemi Basiletti 6-1, 6-3
R3: d. [32] Hailey Baptiste 6-1, 6-2
R4: d. [LL] Nikola Bartunkova 6-2, 6-3
QF: d. [2] Elena Rybakina 2-6, 6-4, 6-4
SF: d. [4] Iga Swiatek 6-4, 2-6, 6-2
F: d. [3] Coco Gauff 6-4, 6-7(3), 6-2

The Internazionali BNL d'Italia champion in 2017-18, No. 7 seed Svitolina reclaimed the Rome crown for a third time after an eight-year gap. The Ukrainian's battling run culminated in a trio of three-set victories over Top 5 opponents, including a 2-hour, 49-minute final defeat of Coco Gauff -- the longest WTA 1000 final of the season. Svitolina's fifth career WTA 1000 title was also her first since returning from maternity leave in 2023.

7. Iga Swiatek, Toronto

R1: bye
R2: d. Sara Bejlek 6-0, 6-3
R3: d. Viktorija Golubic 6-2, 6-1
R4: d. [10] Marta Kostyuk 3-6, 6-1, 6-2
QF: d. [15] Diana Shnaider 6-2, 6-1
SF: d. [9] Elina Svitolina 6-3, 1-6, 6-3
F: d. [2] Elena Rybakina 6-2, 6-3

No. 7 seed Swiatek snapped a 13-month title drought to lift her first National Bank Open trophy -- meaning that of the 15 biggest tournaments (four majors, 10 WTA 1000s and the WTA Finals) currently on the WTA calendar, the Pole is now only missing three: the Australian Open, Dubai and Wuhan. Swiatek's run included two of her four Top 10 wins of 2026.

8. Coco Gauff, Cincinnati

R1: bye
R2: d. Liudmila Samsonova 2-6, 6-4, 6-1
R3: d. [28] Ann Li 6-1, 7-6(3)
R4: d. [22] Marie Bouzkova 6-3, 6-2
QF: d. [10] Marta Kostyuk 6-2, 6-2
SF: d. Sara Bejlek 6-4, 6-1
F: d. [3] Jessica Pegula 6-2, 6-4

No. 4 seed Gauff claimed the Cincinnati Open crown for the second time (following her 2023 title), marking the first time that she has won a trophy at WTA 1000 level or above multiple times. Gauff's final defeat of Jessica Pegula was her fourth of five Top 10 victories so far this year, and marked the first all-American Cincinnati final since 1970.

9. Zheng Qinwen, Beijing

R1: d. [Q] Shi Han 7-6(6), 4-6, 6-2
R2: d. [15] Anna Kalinskaya 6-7(4), 6-4, 3-0 ret.
R3: d. [18] Marie Bouzkova 7-6(4), 4-6, 7-5
R4: d. Alina Charaeva 6-1, 2-6, 6-4
QF: d. [6] Elina Svitolina 6-3, 7-6(6)
SF: d. [13] Elise Mertens 7-5, 6-2
F: d. [4] Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4

Ranked No. 54 but fresh off a run to the US Open quarterfinals as a qualifier, wild card Zheng became the China Open's first home champion with a battling run that included four three-setters and two Top 10 wins. It marked a spectacular return to form -- and to the Top 30 -- for Zheng, who underwent elbow surgery in July 2025 and whose ranking had slipped to No. 160 in June. She dropped 78 games en route to the title -- the second-most of any tour-level champion in the Open Era, only behind Madison Keys (who conceded 87 games on the way to the 2025 Australian Open title).

10. Maja Chwalinska, Wuhan

R1: d. Mayar Sherif 6-3, 6-2
R2: d. Marie Bouzkova 1-6, 6-1, 6-1
R3: d. [10] Iva Jovic 6-4, 6-1
QF: d. Maria Sakkari 6-0, 3-6, 7-5
SF: d. [7] Iga Swiatek 7-5, 6-1
F: d. Sonay Kartal 2-6, 6-4, 6-2

No. 16 seed Chwalinska's spectacular breakthrough season continued at the Dongfeng • Voyah Wuhan Open as the Pole became just the fourth player to win her maiden tour-level title at WTA 1000 level since the format's inception in 2009. Chwalinska, who started the year ranked No. 146 before becoming the first qualifier to reach the Roland Garros final in the Open Era, made her Top 20 debut following her Wuhan title run, which also included her first career Top 10 win -- over compatriot and childhood friend Iga Swiatek in the semifinals.

content.title: Meet your elite eight: A snapshot of the 2026 WTA Finals field
content.description: It's official -- we have our eight-player WTA Finals singles field. Karolina Muchova qualified on Wednesday, and she will join Elena Rybakina, Aryna Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula, Coco Gauff, Mirra Andreeva, Linda Noskova and Elina Svitolina in Indian Wells.

content.body:
Karolina Muchova secured the last WTA Finals qualification berth on Wednesday, and with that we have our elite eight in the desert.

The WTA Finals at Indian Wells will feature three former champions, three newcomers and a wide-open field.

Ahead of the year-end tournament and culmination of the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz season, here's a snapshot of how they got to Indian Wells, and their outlook heading into the finale. 

Elena Rybakina

W-L record: 49-14

Titles won: 3 (Australian Open, Stuttgart, US Open)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 3

Best WTA Finals result: 2025 champion

The skinny: Rybakina was the best player in the world this year. She burst out of the gate, following up her 2025 WTA Finals sweep with an Australian Open title, and ended the Grand Slam season with another major, at the US Open. She beat Aryna Sabalenka in both finals, and the latter win gave her the No. 1 ranking for the first time, ending Sabalenka's 99-week run at the top. She lost her opening match in Beijing and skipped Wuhan, but is playing this week in Ningbo, the last Finals qualifier still in action before Indian Wells.

READ MORE: A US Open champ and new No. 1, Rybakina completes trifecta with a ticket to WTA Finals

Aryna Sabalenka

W-L record: 47-10

Titles won: 3 (Brisbane, Indian Wells, Miami)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 5

Best WTA Finals result: Finalist in 2022 and 2025

The skinny: On the surface, a season without a major title for the first time since 2022 might seem disappointing by Sabalenka’s standards. She still won 47 matches, made a pair of Grand Slam finals and won two WTA 1000 tournaments. Those back-to-back titles in Indian Wells and Miami were the high-water mark of her season, as she became just the fifth player in WTA Tour history to sweep the Sunshine Double. She's had her most success on hard courts, and has historically played very well at the Finals, a tournament she's eager to check off her bucket list. 

She enters the Finals with very little momentum, having lost two of three in Asia, but she should be well-rested.

READ MORE: One result at a time, Aryna Sabalenka keeps ending up at the WTA Finals

Mirra Andreeva

W-L record: 50-16

Titles won: 3 (Adelaide, Linz, Roland Garros)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 0

The skinny: Andreeva has been prolific in 2026, tying Jessica Pegula for the most match-wins (50) on the WTA Tour. The apex of her season was at Roland Garros, where she won her first major. The 19-year-old made four other finals, winning two of them, and her hot hand has continued through the Asian Swing, where she's coming off a run to the final in Beijing. Currently at a career-high No. 3, Andreeva concludes the best season of her career fittingly, at her first WTA Finals. 

READ MORE: '150 percent of your focus': Andreeva on what it will take to compete at the WTA Finals

Jessica Pegula

W-L record: 50-13

Titles won: 2 (Dubai, Charleston)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 4

Best WTA Finals result: 2023 final

The skinny: Pegula was a model of consistency once again in 2026. Tied with Andreeva for the most match-wins on tour, Pegula had the best winning percentage in the world and made five finals. Her two titles came earlier in the season, in Dubai and Charleston, and since April she's gone title-less, losing three consecutive finals in Berlin, Washington, DC and Cincinnati. Pegula has played just one match since the US Open, and should arrive at Indian Wells refreshed after some weeks off. 

READ MORE: How Jessica Pegula’s discipline earned her another trip to the WTA Finals

Coco Gauff

W-L record: 47-15

Titles won: 1 (Cincinnati)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 4

Best WTA Finals result: 2024 champion

The skinny: Gauff's season kicked into gear in Miami, where she reached the final, and she made another WTA 1000 final in Rome a month and a half later. There was further heartbreak late in tournaments, with semifinal runs at Wimbledon and in Toronto, before she got her first title of the year in Cincinnati. She followed that up with a semifinal run in New York, in what was a highly productive Hard-Court Swing. Gauff is so dangerous on hard courts, and the 2024 champion will look to rebound after failing to get out of the group stage last year.

READ MORE: By the numbers: Gauff and Pegula are making WTA Finals history one year at a time

Elina Svitolina

W-L record: 46-14

Titles won: 2 (Auckland, Rome)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 3

Best WTA Finals result: 2018 champion

The skinny: Svitolina returns to the Finals after seven years, and nearly a decade after she made her debut at the year-end tournament.  The 32-year-old won her first 10 matches of the season, including a title in Auckland and a semifinal run in Melbourne, and then won her biggest title of the year on clay, in Rome. She also reached the semis in Indian Wells, Stuttgart and Toronto, to go with a final in Dubai. Back-to-back quarterfinal runs in Beijing and Wuhan show that the 2018 champion is still in form at the tail end of the season. 

READ MORE: WTA Finals flashback: How Svitolina turned a shaky stretch in Asia into the biggest title of her career

Karolina Muchova

W-L record: 40-11

Titles won: 2 (Doha, Bad Homburg)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 0

The skinny: It's hard to believe that when Muchova won the Qatar TotalEnergies Open in February, it was only her second career title, and first since 2019. It was the biggest title of her career, and it set the tone for the rest of the season, which included a second title in Bad Homburg and a runner-up finish at Wimbledon. That run to the final propelled her to a career-high No. 6 in the world. Muchova also made semifinals in Brisbane and Miami, and a final in Stuttgart. With her all-court game, athleticism and ability to hit any shot from any angle, she's one of the toughest outs in tennis.

READ MORE: Karolina Muchova secures final qualification place for FAGE WTA Finals Indian Wells

Linda Noskova

W-L record: 35-15

Titles won: 2 (Berlin, Wimbledon)

Previous WTA Finals appearances: 0

The skinny: Noskova's breakthrough came at Wimbledon, where she won her first career major as a No. 9 seed. Though the title was surprising, anyone who had been paying attention could see that she was a threat on grass, having beaten Pegula in the Berlin final a couple weeks earlier. But the 21-year-old proved that she can win on all surfaces in 2026, reaching the semis at Indian Wells earlier in the year and the quarterfinals of the US Open in September. Noskova withdrew from Wuhan with a left calf injury, but she should have enough time to recover for Indian Wells.

READ MORE: The first-timers who won the WTA Finals: Could Andreeva or Noskova be next?

content.body:
The final WTA 1000 tournament of the season has not disappointed. 

With a shortened format, there have been a flurry of incredible matches each day, accompanied by some of the most varied, creative shot-making we've seen all season.

We've rounded up our five favorite shots from the Dongfeng • Voyah Wuhan Open through the quarterfinals. Check them out, and make sure to vote for your WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz shot of the week below.

Maja Chwalinska's pinpoint right-handed lob

Chwalinska has had one of the best weeks of her career, and proven that her game can be just as effective off the clay as it is on it.

She's hit an array of remarkable, inventive shots through her first four wins, but none have been more impressive than this. Stretched wide by Maria Sakkari, the left-handed Chwalinska had to use her right hand to keep the ball in play, and the result was a perfectly weighted lob with her non-dominant hand. She then finished off the point with a backhand winner on the line.

Chwalinska won the match 6-3, 3-6, 7-5 to advance to her first career WTA 1000 semifinal.

Jelena Ostapenko's forehand slice winner on the run

Leading 4-1, 15-0 in the second set against Diana Shnaider, Ostapenko sprinted across the court to retrieve a backhand, and responded with a running forehand slice winner down the line.

In total control, and clearly feeling her shots, on the next point she hit a return winner into the same corner, this time a backhand.

Ostapenko won 7-6 (6), 6-1 to advance to the semifinals.

Diana Shnaider's wrong-footing forehand

Just incredible stuff from both players here, in one of the most athletic and reflexive points of the tournament.

After Shnaider hit a volley off of Karolina Muchova's forehand, she won the cat-and-mouse point with a wrong-footing forehand.

Shnaider won the match 7-5, 6-3.

Jelena Ostapenko's drop shot winner on match point

Does it get more daring, and clutch, than this? On Jessica Pegula's third match point, Ostapenko stayed aggressive, hitting a barrage of forehands to keep her behind the baseline. Then she pulled the string and hit a drop shot, her first of the day, for the winner to stay alive in the match. 

Ostapenko ultimately came back to win, completing the improbable comeback 2-6, 7-6 (7), 6-3 in one of the biggest upsets of the tournament.

Karolina Muchova's leaping behind-the-back overhead

Another week, another magic trick from the audacious and endlessly entertaining Muchova.

After Caty McNally brought Muchova in with the drop shot, Muchova pushed the American into the corner with a running forehand. McNally hit a very solid backhand lob, but Muchova tracked it and won the point, as only she can, with a leaping, twisting, behind-the-back overhead.

Muchova won the match 3-6, 7-6 (1), 7-6 (4).

content.title: Around Wuhan: Muchova's impressive tiebreak feat; Jovic, Chwalinska set to meet
content.description: Around the grounds in Wuhan, Karolina Muchova maintained her perfect 10-0 tiebreak record to the season in a gritty comeback win over Caty McNally. Maja Chwalinska also came back, but in contrasting fashion, and is set to meet Iva Jovic in the third round.

content.body:
WUHAN -- No. 6 seed Karolina Muchova and No. 16 seed Maja Chwalinska both needed to win in comeback fashion in their Dongfeng • Voyah Wuhan Open second-round matches Wednesday, but the two could not be more different. 

For Muchova, she went toe-to-toe with qualifier Caty McNally, who was seeking her third career top 10 win on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz. McNally dominated the first set, and the match went down to the wire in the second and third sets, both requiring a tiebreak -- a situation that Muchova has thrived in this season.

The Czech is 10-0 in tiebreaks this season, becoming the first player this century to win their first 10 tiebreaks in a single season. Sanchez Vicario (2000) and Maria Sakkari (2020) both won their first nine.

Two of Muchova's 10 came in her 3-6, 7-6(1), 7-6(4) win over McNally. Last week in Beijing, she also won two more sets in tiebreaks, once in her opening match vs. Katie Boulter and the other against Naomi Osaka in a fourth-round match that saw her need nine match points to win. 

"I actually knew that this year I'm doing pretty great in tiebreaks," Muchova said to press. "In my head, I try to tell myself, 'Okay, it's tiebreak, it's my thing.' Kind of give myself confidence and try to play aggressive in my game from the start of both of the tiebreaks, and I think it is just paying off.

"Obviously, you never know in a breaker, and I think I catch the start of it and hit some good shots, winners, good serves. When you're a bit ahead in a tiebreak, you play until seven points so then I just felt closer and was more confident."

The victory also marked Muchova's 14th three-set win in 2026, the most she's had in a single season. She also has recorded eight come back wins, too, more than the last two years combined.

While Muchova recognizes that she's played significantly more matches this season compared to years past, she also attributed the reasoning to her grit on court. 

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

"I just obviously try to fight in every match and not just leave it there," Muchova said. "Today, I didn't feel so great in the first set. I wasn't feeling myself. And I think in the second set, when I broke her serve, I kind of like switched and I locked myself in a bubble and was swinging more freely.

"I just wanted to basically, not leave it there, just fight and try to get that win. That's what I try to do in every match. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't, but I'm glad that this year I have more numbers that did work."

Muchova is set to face [11] Diana Shnaider to begin play on Center Court Thursday. 

Chwalinska wins 12 of last 14 games vs. Bouzkova

Marie Bouzkova seemed to be well on her way to a spot in Wuhan's third round with a 6-1 first set against Chwalinska.

Then, the tables turned as Chwalinska each of the next two sets in a topsy-turvy 1-6, 6-1, 6-1 win. She's into her first Round of 16 at a WTA 1000 event, and will next face Iva Jovic. 

Jovic's path to the third round was much more streamlined in a 6-4, 6-1 win over Dayana Yastremska after a first-round bye. The 18-year-old American has seen the rise of Chwalinska ever since the Pole's breakthrough at Roland Garros. 

"She's had an incredible year and a big breakthrough," Jovic said. "Obviously, making finals of the Slam is a dream. I think it'll be a good match. She's definitely a crafty player. We've only practiced together once or twice, maybe, so it'll be interesting. We'll see who plays their game better."

content.title: Week in review: Zheng returns to glory, and makes history, in Beijing
content.description: Zheng Qinwen made history as the first Chinese player to win the China Open, then celebrated her milestone win with some karaoke. Plus, Nikola Bartunkova had the breakthrough of her career. All that and more in the latest WTA week in review.

Zheng Qinwen makes history with China Open win in first title since 2024

content.body:
History was made in Beijing this past week, as Zheng Qinwen became the first Chinese player to win the China Open.

It was a dream tournament for Zheng, and a career highlight. But she wasn't the only player who shined in Beijing's second week. A 20-year-old cemented herself as one of the brightest rising stars on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz and two players qualified for the WTA Finals for the first time. Plus, we were treated to one of the most thrilling matches of the season.

Here's everything you need to know about what went down on tour last week, and the most important takeaways. 

Star of the Week

Zheng Qinwen

After some time away, Zheng Qinwen has officially returned to the upper tier of the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz.

Zheng won the biggest WTA title of her career, and her first since 2024, with an inspired performance in Beijing. And boy, did she earn it. In what has become a trend for the Olympic gold medalist, she won four consecutive three-setters to reach the quarterfinals, then upset sixth-seeded Elina Svitolina and 13th-seeded Elise Mertens to reach the final. She picked up another huge upset in the championship match, knocking off fourth-seeded Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4 for her first WTA 1000 title.

Zheng, who got into the main draw as a wild card, is the lowest-ranked player ever to win the China Open, which dates back to 1994. (There was an eight-year hiatus between 1996 and 2004.) And she did it with an incredible display of power and controlled aggression. She had 243 winners in Beijing, the most of any player at any tournament since Aryna Sabalenka's 247 at the 2023 Australian Open. And her 51 aces trailed only Elena Rybakina's 54 at the US Open.

Speaking of the US Open, Zheng has now won 14 of her last 15 matches since the season's last major, where she reached the quarterfinals as a qualifier.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Breakthrough of the Week

Nikola Bartunkova

Coming into this tournament, 20-year-old Nikola Bartunkova had never been past the round of 16 at a WTA 1000 tournament. But the surging Czech star blew past that stage in Beijing, reaching the semifinals. She picked up the second and third Top 10 wins of her career along the way, upsetting Sabalenka in straight sets in the third round and then Karolina Muchova in the quarterfinals (more on that below).

After starting the season at No. 126 in the PIF WTA Rankings, she's now up to a career-high No. 29.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Best Match of the Week

Karolina Muchova d. Naomi Osaka, China Open round of 16

Muchova trailed by a break in both the first and third sets, but came back to outlast Naomi Osaka 7-5, 1-6, 7-6 (7) in a match that lasted 2 hours and 52 minutes. 

Muchova trailed 4-1 in the first set and 3-1 in the decider, and failed to convert triple match point at 5-4 in the third after five missed opportunities. She had three more match points in the tiebreaker, and finally clinched the match on her ninth match point with a backhand volley winner.

"I was shaking," a relieved Muchova said after the match.

Biggest Upset of the Week

Nikola Bartunkova d. Karolina Muchova, China Open quarterfinals

Jubilation was replaced with frustration in Muchova's next match, a dispiriting 6-3, 6-0 loss to Bartunkova in the quarterfinals.

As impressive as the win was for Bartunkova, what made it all the more surprising was the efficiency in which she delivered it. Bartunkova dropped just three games, including a second-set bagel, in just 67 minutes.

Within 20 minutes she was up 5-0 in the opener, and after Muchova fought back to make it interesting, Bartunkova won the final seven games to close out the dominant win.

Biggest Mover of the Week

Zheng Qinwen

Zheng rose 31 spots in the PIF WTA Rankings, to No. 23. Andreeva, 19, rose two spots to a career-high No. 3.

Social Moment of the Week

The karaoke queen

Biggest WTA title of her career? Check. History made on home soil? Check. Birthday week? Check. Return to the top 25? Check. Seems like as good a time as any to do some celebratory karaoke.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Tennis (@tennischannel)

And this wasn't the first time Zheng has shown off her karaoke skills. Cut to the United Cup two years ago.

Best Shot of the Week

Sara Bejlek's pass down the line

Sara Bejlek's speed and anticipation are her hallmarks, and they won her this point against Osaka.

Leading 4-3 in the first set, on Osaka's serve, Bejlek returned a combination of powerful backhands and forehands before winning the point with a remarkable pass down the line.

Must-Listen Podcast of the Week

Eala gets deep with Sharapova

Alexandra Eala was a guest on the "Pretty Tough with Maria Sharapova" podcast, and Eala discussed in great detail her relationship with perfection, navigating public opinion and managing pressure, and what makes her feel pretty and tough, among many other topics.

Check out their conversation below. 

Best Stat of the Week

15 hours

Zheng's four three-setters in seven matches, including four tiebreakers, kept her on court for 15 hours and 16 minutes. That's the most time spent on court by any player at any tournament this year, and the most since Opta began tracking total time spent on court in 2023. 

WTA Finals Update of the Week

Noskova, Andreeva punch their tickets

We have two more qualifiers! Andreeva and Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova have officially qualified for the WTA Finals at Indian Wells. 

They will both be making their WTA Finals singles debuts. (Andreeva qualified alongside Diana Shnaider in doubles last year.)

They join Sabalenka and Rybakina in the field, with four singles spots still up for grabs.

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

content.description: Nikola Bartunkova won an inter-generational clash of Czech compatriots against Karolina Muchova in just 67 minutes in the China Open quarterfinals, scoring her third Top 10 win and advancing to her first WTA 1000 semifinal.

content.body:
No. 26 seed Nikola Bartunkova reached the first WTA 1000 semifinal of her career on Thursday, defeating No. 7 Karolina Muchova 6-3, 6-0 in 67 minutes at the China Open.

In an inter-generational matchup of Czech compatriots who train at Prague’s Štvanice club, the 20-year-old Bartunkova won the first five and final seven games against the 30-year-old Muchova. It was her third career win over a Top 10 opponent, following victories over Belinda Bencic at the Australian Open and Aryna Sabalenka in the third round in Beijing. Bartunkova had previously reached tour-level semifinals in Guadalajara in 2025 and Monterrey in 2026.

Bartunkova, who ended 2025 ranked No. 130 and has climbed to No. 34 this week, will make her Top 30 debut following Beijing. She will bid to reach her first career final against No. 4 seed Mirra Andreeva, who narrowly escaped No. 19 Ekaterina Alexandrova 7-6(4), 7-6(3)

Despite her steep upward trajectory in 2026, Bartunkova's run in Beijing has taken her by surprise.

"For sure [I didn't expect it] before this tournament," she said in her press conference. "I played lot of practices with top players -- [iga] Swiatek, [Coco] Gauff, others. Maybe it helps little bit. [It] was one week before the tournament. I tried to play a lot of practices, lot of matches. I think that was the reason I had good preparation for this tournament. So yeah, I had confidence. But honestly I didn't expect these results."

How did Bartunkova pull off the upset?

As Bartunkova has risen through the rankings this year, her combination of power and touch has drawn frequent comparisons to Muchova herself. Ahead of their first meeting, the question was whether Muchova’s greater experience -- particularly during the most consistent season of her career, which has included titles in Doha and Bad Homburg and a second Grand Slam final at Wimbledon -- would give her the edge.

"I follow her a lot," said Bartunkova of Muchova. "I have also similar style like her, playing lot of drop shots, volleys. I like her because she's also a great human being."

Off court, there was respect. On court, Bartunkova didn't permit Muchova to get her game going. The younger player has every shot in the book, and a first-strike mentality to use them as quickly as possible in the point. She broke in the second game with four consecutive returns fired deep at Muchova's feet, drawing an error each time. In the fourth game, she used her drop shot as an audacious plus-one winner en route to breaking again.

The drop shot was also the setup for Bartunkova's two best points of the match -- a stretch backhand volley as she moved up 4-0 in the first set, and a perfect volleyed lob at the same stage of the second.

Intent on being the first to break open each point, Bartunkova did not let herself get drawn into extended rallies and within 20 minutes led 5-0.

"Today I was really aggressive," she said. "I [wasn't] very nervous. Yeah, try to put my best tennis. I did it."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

What were Muchova's best chances to turn the match around?

At 5-0 in the first set, Bartunkova was in such complete command that she even pulled off an absurd backhand slice winner that caught Muchova off guard yet again. But a handful of forehand errors allowed Muchova to get on the board, and closing out the set proved a tricky task.

Bartunkova has squandered a number of significant leads this summer -- 6-2, 4-0 against Sabalenka in Berlin; 5-1 in the third set and four match points against Lanlana Tararudee in Prague; 4-2 in the third set against Amanda Anisimova in Toronto; 6-1, 3-0 against Elise Mertens in Monterrey. Surely aware of that pattern, Muchova played her most aggressive tennis to claw back three games and fend off five set points.

But the gulf was too much to make up -- and, as Bartunkova said, her nerves didn't come into play. Up a sixth set point, Muchova offered up a drop shot that landed closer to the service line than the net, and Bartunkova stayed calm to swat it away for a winner.

There were no similar chances in the second set. Bartunkova leapt out to an early lead again and this time didn't let up, tallying 19 winners to Muchova's 12. Muchova faded in the home stretch as her unforced error count reached 37.

content.body:
At the season’s most recent Grand Slam, the US Open, the top five seeds reached the quarterfinals. The top four advanced to the semifinals, with the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds meeting for the title.

Beijing has gone in the other direction. At the second-to-last 1000-level event of the season on the WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz, the top two seeds are already out, and only one of the top five remains with the quarterfinals set.

Among the final eight is an unseeded home favorite, a pair of Grand Slam champions, several tried-and-true veterans and an up-and-comer having the best tournament of her career.

Here's what you need to know about the matchups ahead of the China Open quarterfinals.

Zheng Qinwen vs. [6] Elina Svitolina

First meeting

Zheng is becoming awfully familiar with three-set matches. She won four straight three-setters to reach the US Open quarterfinals, then lost another three-set match there.

The pattern has continued at her home tournament in Beijing, where all four of her matches have gone the distance. The unseeded World No. 54 has come back from a set down twice and upset No. 15 seed Anna Kalinskaya and No. 18 seed Marie Bouzkova. On Wednesday, she defeated Alina Charaeva 6-1, 2-6, 6-4.

It's been a smoother, and less physically demanding, tournament for Elina Svitolina. The sixth seed has played one fewer match after receiving a first-round bye, and has won six consecutive sets with ease after dropping her first to Katerina Siniakova last week.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Surprisingly, despite both players being veterans with a track record of success, this will be their first career meeting. Zheng will surely be buoyed by her home crowd as she looks to make her first semifinal since June 2025, at Queen's Club. Svitolina most recently made the semis in Toronto, in August, and is in pursuit of her third title of the year.

[13] Elise Mertens vs. [8] Iga Swiatek

Swiatek leads the head-to-head 2-0

Elise Mertens has had to work for her quarterfinal berth. Her first-round match against Katie Volynets was a doozy. Mertens was in total control, leading 6-0, 3-0, with four opportunities to take a 4-0 lead in that second set.

But before she could comprehend what went wrong, she found herself down a break in the third. She rallied to win that match 6-0, 4-6, 7-5 in just under three hours. The World No. 19 bore down late in her next match as well, coming from 2-0 down in the decider to beat Jelena Ostapenko.

Surprisingly, her most comfortable win of the tournament came on Wednesday against Coco Gauff, whom she had never beaten in five tries. Mertens closed the match out strong, winning 10 of her last 11 service points and closing out the 6-3, 6-3 win with an ace.

Iga Swiatek had a close call in her second match, somehow finding a way to beat Donna Vekic after trailing 6-4, 5-2. But her fourth-round match against Iva Jovic was never in doubt, an authoritative 6-1, 6-3 win in which "everything was working," as Swiatek accurately put it.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Swiatek has never dropped a set to Mertens. In their lone match on hard courts, in Miami last year, Swiatek beat Mertens 7-6 (2), 6-1.

[19] Ekaterina Alexandrova vs. [4] Mirra Andreeva

Alexandrova leads the head-to-head 2-0

Ekaterina Alexandrova has pulled off a couple of big upsets in Beijing, coming from a set down against 11th seed Diana Shnaider and following that up with a commanding win over fifth-seeded Linda Noskova. Alexandrova wasn't broken against the Wimbledon champion, dropping just four games in a little over an hour.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

She'll face a well-rested and in-form Andreeva, who lost her first set in Beijing to Yuan Yue. It's been smooth sailing since then, though. She rallied to win the next 12 games for the three-set win, the rare double bagel on the back end, then breezed past unseeded Polina Kudermetova and Daria Snigur to book her spot in the quarterfinals.

After the 6-2, 6-2 win over Snigur, Andreeva took to the practice courts -- not her choice, she clarified -- to work on returns. She'll certainly need a strong return game against Alexandrova, who hit six aces and won 88 percent of her first-serve points against Noskova.

Andreeva will be the favorite, considering her higher ranking and more recent success, but Alexandrova comes in with the confidence of a 2-0 head-to-head advantage. This will be their first meeting on hard courts, though. Alexandrova beat Andreeva in straight sets on clay last year, and beat her again on grass, in Bad Homburg, back in June. 

[7] Karolina Muchova vs. [26] Nikola Bartunkova 

First meeting

What a fun encounter this should be between two wildly talented Czechs, one an established veteran and the other a rising up-and-comer.

Karolina Muchova and Nikola Bartunkova have both taken dramatic paths to the Beijing quarterfinals. After Muchova beat Katie Boulter in straight sets, she came from a set down to knock off Liudmila Samsonova.

But that was just an appetizer for her next match, a nearly-three-hour marathon against Naomi Osaka that came down to a third-set tiebreak. Muchova was down breaks in both the first and third sets, and eventually clinched the match on her ninth match point. Her much-improved backhand let her down late in the third set, but she stayed aggressive with it, firing a backhand winner down the line to set up the ninth match point.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

As for Bartunkova, she's fresh off the biggest win of her career, a 6-4, 6-3 upset of second-seeded Aryna Sabalenka. She then avoided the post-upset hangover, beating Sinja Kraus 6-0, 4-6, 6-3 to book a spot in a WTA 1000 quarterfinal for the first time.

Despite their 10-year age gap, and having never played on tour, they know each others' games well. They train at the same club in Prague and are frequent practice partners. Expect plenty of finesse, touch and exceptional shot-making in this one.

content.description: Karolina Muchova came from a break down in both the first and third sets, then needed nine match points to get over the line against Naomi Osaka in the China Open fourth round.

content.body:
No. 7 seed Karolina Muchova came through a spectacular fourth-round tilt at the China Open on Tuesday, denying No. 12 seed Naomi Osaka from a break down in both the first and third sets and eventually sealing her ninth match point to advance 7-5, 1-6, 7-6(7) in 2 hours and 52 minutes.

Muchova, who trailed 4-1 in the opener and 3-1 in the decider, held triple-match point at 5-4 in the third set on Osaka's serve -- but was unable to take a total of five opportunities to seal victory in that game. In the ensuing tiebreak, the Czech player missed another three match points, but converted the ninth in style with a delicate backhand volley winner.

"I honestly didn't even believe I will finish the match," Muchova said in her on-court interview. "So many match points, I didn't know how many. After a match point I was like, 'OK, I'm going for it,' but then I think she always played great and steady, and didn't make mistakes -- unlike me, unfortunately! I was shaking. I'm happy that I made the last volley and it was really so close. Naomi could be standing here. It's me, and I'm really grateful for it."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

In the eighth edition of the pair's six-year rivalry, Muchova backed up two grass-court victories this year to improve to 5-3 overall against Osaka -- though she still trails 3-2 on outdoor hard courts. She booked her place in her fourth quarterfinal at WTA 1000 level or above this season, following her Doha title, Wimbledon final run and Miami semifinal showing. 

Here are the key takeaways from Muchova's win:

Her backhand nearly lost her the match ... but ultimately won it for her

In previous seasons, Muchova's drive backhand has been an area of vulnerability for her -- both more prone to breaking down and less lethal than her forehand wing. She's levelled up on that side in 2026, one of the reasons this has been the most consistent of her career to date.

But as she tried to close Osaka out, it nearly let her down again. She squandered three of the five match points she held at 5-4 with backhand unforced errors -- Osaka saved the other two with an ace and a service winner. Another backhand sprayed wide enabled Osaka to hold that game, and another dumped in the net wasted her seventh match point. (Match points six and eight were lost on forehand unforced errors.)

No wonder that, at 7-7 in the tiebreak, Osaka began targeting that wing exclusively -- and nor did the 2019 champion hold back as she pummelled it at full force. Muchova managed to withstand all the pace, though -- and then find the space she needed to redirect it for a winner down the line to bring up her ninth and final match point.

"I think I was solid from the backhand side today," Muchova said. "I feel like all the players are hitting to my backhand side. But I'd say it was a shot that won the match for me today."

Muchova remains perfect in third-set tiebreaks this year

The result extended Muchova's record in third-set tiebreaks this year to a perfect 3-0 -- she also edged Ajla Tomljanovic 4-6, 6-1, 7-6(5) in the Brisbane second round, her first match of the season, and then saved a match point to deny Coco Gauff 6-2, 1-6, 7-6[10] in the Wimbledon semifinals.

The only other player with a 3-0 record in deciding tiebreaks this year is Rabat champion Petra Marcinko (who won her trio against Camila Osorio in Auckland, Yelyzaveta Kotliar in Rabat and Antonia Ruzic in Eastbourne). No player has won more than three deciding tiebreaks at tour level this year; Anna Kalinskaya has also won three, but has lost two as well.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Muchova's strong third-set tiebreak performance isn't new -- the 30-year-old owns an 8-3 career record in them at tour level, dating back to 2019. She hasn't lost a third-set tiebreak since the second round of the 2023 Australian Open, when she fell 6-7(1), 6-2, 7-6[6] to Danielle Collins.

That's a contrast to Osaka's 2-6 career record in deciding tiebreaks. The four-time major champion has not won one since the 2019 Stuttgart quarterfinals, when she edged Donna Vekic 6-3, 4-6, 7-6(4).

In this one, Muchova acknowledged that she "got a bit lucky" -- at 6-6, Osaka hammered a forehand return crosscourt as she sought to reach match point for the first time. Muchova only just got her racquet on the ball in response -- and her forehand dribbled over the net cord for a fortuitous steal.

Muchova faces a crafty Czech in her own mold next

Next up for Muchova is an all-Czech derby against No. 26 seed Nikola Bartunkova, who backed up her third-round upset of Aryna Sabalenka with a 6-0, 4-6, 6-3 defeat of Sinja Kraus to make her first WTA 1000 quarterfinal. It'll be the first time the pair have played each other, and an intriguing matchup. The 20-year-old Bartunkova's potent blend of power and finesse has drawn plenty of comparisons with Muchova as she's risen from No. 126 at the start of the year to her current career high of No. 34.

Muchova has been aware of Bartunkova's talent for a while longer. They both train at the same club in Prague, and are frequent practise partners on tour.

"I'm not surprised it could be a Czech match," she said. "It's on every tournament, in all the rounds you can play a Czech player. It's not really surprising anymore, I would say ... I never played Niki. She is a crafty player."

content.body:
No lead was safe during the first week of the China Open.

The same could be said for the top two seeds and presumptive favorites.

We've also seen a trio of breakthroughs in Beijing, from players who could very well be contending for titles in the not-too-distant future (if not immediately).

As the 96-player draw has begun to whittle down to eight, there have been no shortage of compelling storylines and memorable moments, and more than a few plot twists. Before the second-to-last WTA 1000 tournament of 2026 heads toward its conclusion, we reflect on the notable happenings from an eventful first week of play.

Star of the Week

Alina Charaeva

Alina Charaeva's week looked to be over before it started, as she fell behind a set and a break to Yuliia Starodubtseva in the first round. She fought her way back in that one, rallying for a 5-7, 7-5, 6-2 win in 3 hours and 12 minutes. 

That alone would have been a career highlight, as it was her first WTA 1000 win. But she followed it up with the moment of her career, knocking off World No. 1 Elena Rybakina in the second round (much more on that below). She came from a set down in that match, too.

The World No. 118 carried that momentum into her third-round match, where she had a far easier time with Sonay Kartal 6-4, 6-1.

Charaeva could make her Top 100 debut next week even if she loses her next match, though it will depend on other players' results. But defeating Zheng Qinwen in the fourth round would guarantee it.

Breakthrough of the Week

Sun Xinran

She only won two matches, but 16-year-old Sun Xinran made quite an impression in her WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz debut.

Playing in front of her home fans, the US Open girls' champion and junior World No. 1 took nine of 10 games from Eva Lys in her opener, before Lys retired with a foot injury.

In her next match, Sun upset 27th seed Cristina Bucsa 6-4, 7-5 to pick up the first Top 50 win of her young career. That set up a match against fourth-ranked Coco Gauff. Sun played her tough in the first set before Gauff pulled away for a 7-5, 6-1 win.

Afterwards, Gauff was very complimentary of the rising star.

"She's an incredible player," Gauff said. "I knew going in it was going to be a tough match. The junior career that she's had is incredible, and obviously she's going to do great at this level.

"I think this is the first of many matches on this court and many matches that we will play against each other. I'm looking forward to the future matchups we have."

Honorable mention: Nikola Bartunkova, who upset No. 2 Aryna Sabalenka and is into her first career WTA 1000 quarterfinal.

Biggest Upset of the Week

Alina Charaeva d. Elena Rybakina, second round

How big was this upset? Consider this: Only once before had a player lost her first match after securing the No. 1 ranking. Charaeva also became just the ninth player outside the Top 100 to beat a World No. 1, and the lowest-ranked player ever to beat a World No. 1 after being a set down.

It was just the 17th tour-level match of the 24-year-old Armenian's career. Prior to beating Rybakina, her best win came against then-No. 31 Wang Xinyu earlier this year.

"Of course, I was just trying to enjoy, to not be so nervous," Charaeva admitted. "It wasn't possible. I was so nervous anyway."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Best Match of the Week

Elise Mertens d. Katie Volynets, second round

What an odd match this was. Elise Mertens absolutely dominated early on, taking the first nine games for a commanding 6-0, 3-0 lead. She then had four opportunities to go up 4-0 in the second, with a double bagel looking like a very real possibility.

Then Katie Volynets flipped the script abruptly. She stole the second and went up a break in the third before Mertens found her footing again, escaping with a 6-0, 4-6, 7-5 win in 2 hours and 54 minutes.

Best Comeback of the Week

Iga Swiatek d. Donna Vekic, third round

Late in her second set against Donna Vekic, Iga Swiatek appeared to be joining Sabalenka and Elena Rybakina as multiple-Slam-champion casualties in Beijing. Swiatek trailed 6-4, 5-2, but broke twice to level the match at 5-all. She then took the tiebreaker without dropping a point.

They exchanged breaks to open the decider, and after breaking again for 3-2, Swiatek took the final three games for the 4-6, 7-6 (0), 6-2 win.

Best Shot of the Week

Karolina Muchova's 360-degree pickup and pass

At 3-all in the first-set tiebreaker, Katie Boulter returned Karolina Muchova's serve just beyond the baseline. The Wimbledon runner-up responded with an improbable 360-degree spinning pickup. Boulter got to it and beautifully flicked it toward the sideline. Muchova read it, shuffled to the alley and won the point with a perfectly-angled pass.

As good, and as smooth, as it gets. Muchova won the match 7-6 (3), 6-1.

Social Moment of the Week

WTA stars take to the red carpet

Before play began in Beijing, a collection of WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz stars had the opportunity to relax, laugh and mingle at the player party.

They also showcased an array of stunning looks and styles on the red carpet. Check out all the photos here.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Biggest Off-Court News of the Week

Equal prize money milestone

It was a quite a busy week off the court.

The WTA was thrilled to announce that in 2027, all combined WTA 1000 events will award equal prize money for the first time. The 2027 calendar was also revealed, including a new WTA 250 tournament in Manila, Philippines. 

To read more about calendar changes and the new Tournament Investment Fund, click here.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Most Dominant Performance of the Week

Daria Snigur d. Taylah Preston, third round

Forty-seven minutes ...47 minutes! That's how long it took for Daria Snigur to beat Taylah Preston 6-1, 6-0 in the China Open third round.

Best Stat of the Week

Points to winners ratio

In Sabalenka's 6-1, 6-3 win over Renata Zarazua, Sabalenka hit 36 winners -- two more than Zarazua's total points won (34).

content.body:
It was a short week, with the China Open in Beijing not getting underway until Wednesday. But with a stacked 96-player draw, there was no shortage of matches -- and no shortage of incredible shots.

We've combed through the early rounds in Beijing and picked our five favorite shots. Which do you think was the best? Check them out below, and vote for your WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz shot of the week at the bottom.

Sara Bejlek's running forehand crosscourt lob

Sara Bejlek was a human highlight reel in her Beijing debut. Leading 4-2 in the first set, she hit a running forehand crosscourt lob that landed just inside the baseline. 

Then in the first point of the second set, after a lengthy rally, she hit a drop shot to force Maddison Inglis in. After Inglis dumped it back over the net, Bejlek put her away with the forehand winner.

Bejlek won the match 6-3, 7-5.

Karolina Muchova's 360-degree pickup and pass

Karolina Muchova routinely pulls off shots that we've never seen before. She did it again on Friday, against Katie Boulter.

At 3-all in the first-set tiebreaker, Boulter returned Muchova's serve just beyond the baseline. The Wimbledon runner-up responded with an improbable 360-degree spinning pickup. Boulter got to it and beautifully flicked it toward the sideline. Muchova read it, shuffled to the alley and won the point with a perfectly-angled pass.

Muchova won the tiebreaker and rolled in the second set for the 7-6 (3), 6-1 win.

Linda Noskova's pinpoint lobs

While we're on the subject of Czech shot-makers, Linda Noskova showed off pinpoint precision against Elena-Gabriela Ruse. At 2-0, 15-all in the first set, Noskova hit a drop shot to bring Ruse in, then hit a lob on the short hop that sailed over her head and landed just in front of the line. 

Later in the set, with Noskova leading 3-0, she hit a running forehand lob that floated just past Ruse's outstretched racquet.

Noskova went on to win 6-4, 6-1.

Ekaterina Alexandrova's forehand flicks at full stretch

Ekaterina Alexandrova had the touch on Friday against Aliaksandra Sasnovich.

In the first game of the match, on ad point, Alexandrova flicked a crosscourt winner that snuck over the net. Later in the set, at 4-0, 30-15, she pulled it off again, a mirror image of the first winner.

Alexandrova won 6-1, 6-4.

Sun Xinran's drop shot winner

Sun Xinran wasted little time showing fans why she's the junior World No. 1.

Leading Eva Lys 2-1 in the first set in her WTA debut, Sun ended a punishing 22-stroke rally with a drop shot winner, pulling the string after repeated blows from the baseline.

Three games later, the power was back on display. The US Open junior champion ended an even longer rally -- this one 23 shots -- with a backhand winner into the corner.

The 16-year-old was leading Lys 6-1, 3-0 when Lys retired with a foot injury.

content.title: Anatomy of a hot shot: Karolina Muchova on her 360-degree spin in Beijing
content.description: Karolina Muchova came up with an absurd piece of athletic artistry (again) in the China Open second round. But have these hot shots become so commonplace for the Czech that she now finds them routine and unmemorable?

related.label: Former champ Osaka survives stern test from Timofeeva in Beijing

Maja Chwalinska’s feather-light finish earns September Shot of the Month

content.body:
Is it possible to play so many hot shots that they become routine -- unmemorable, even?

Apparently so for Karolina Muchova. With her second-round match against Katie Boulter at the China Open poised at 3-3 in the first-set tiebreak, the Czech came up with some dizzying wizardry -- a full 360-degree spinning pickup, then a finely angled pass at full stretch past the flailing Briton.

It wasn't just a sensational piece of athletic artistry, but the key point of the match. It effectively ended Boulter's impact on the contest -- Muchova did not drop another point in the tiebreak, then ran away with the second set for a 7-6(3), 6-1 victory. Most players would be dining out on it for weeks, if not years, to come.

But asked about it afterwards, the two-time major finalist had no idea what reporters were talking about. "My spin shot?" she asked, quizzically. She had to be shown a clip of it to jog her memory.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Once Muchova was watching it back, though, she was able to explain how she pulled it off -- as much as one can explain genius in mere human language, at any rate.

"[I feel I'm] quite well under, like on my feet," she recalled. "I feel like this was the only way to kind of pick it up. It went naturally because I had it behind my body, so my body went that way. It's not that I was thinking about it ahead. I would rather hit nice easy backhand volley, but this was out of it. I'm happy that I managed to win that shot."

It's simple -- and maybe even forgettable -- when you put it like that. But most importantly, there'll be the chance to see what else Muchova can come up with in Beijing: the No. 7 seed has advanced to face No. 29 seed Liudmila Samsonova in the third round.

content.title: Czechia wins 12th Billie Jean King Cup title with sweep of Ukraine
content.description: Once again, Czechia sits atop the tennis landscape after Karolina Muchova and Linda Noskova delivered the two wins needed to beat Ukraine for the Billie Jean King Cup title.
content.body:
Czechia remains the country to beat in the Billie Jean King Cup after Karolina Muchova and Linda Noskova won in straight sets Sunday in Shenzhen to clinch a 2-0 victory over Ukraine and a 12th title.

Muchova opened the final with a 6-2, 6-3 win over Anhelina Kalinina. Noskova then completed the sweep, holding off Elina Svitolina 6-3, 7-6 (5) in the second singles match.

The title is Czechia’s first since 2018 and gives Barbora Strycova a victory in her first Billie Jean King Cup Finals as captain. Strycova was part of the Czech Republic teams that won six titles between 2011 and 2018.

Czechia has now won 12 of its 13 Billie Jean King Cup final appearances.

Muchova, the World No. 8, took charge early against Kalinina. She broke twice in the opening set and did not face much pressure on serve, wrapping it up in a little more than 30 minutes.

Kalinina had won both singles and doubles in Ukraine’s quarterfinal victory over Belgium, then defeated Tyra Grant to begin Ukraine’s semifinal win over Italy. But Muchova found another level in the final. After moving ahead 3-2 in the second set, she kept Kalinina pinned behind the baseline, while her own serve gave the Ukrainian little to work with.

Kalinina won only three points on return in the second set. Muchova closed the match with a forehand winner.

Noskova and Svitolina followed with a match worthy of a final.

Svitolina earned the first break of the match for a 3-1 lead, but Noskova answered in the next game after racing to a 0-40 advantage. She then won the final five games of the set to take it 6-3.

The second set was tighter and, oddly enough, offered no break points. None of the 12 games reached deuce, leaving a tiebreak to decide whether Czechia would need a doubles match.

At 3-3, Svitolina hit consecutive aces to level the score at the changeover. Noskova responded by earning three championship points. Svitolina saved the first two, but Noskova converted the third, pushing her wide before driving a forehand into the open court.

Noskova dropped to the court as Strycova and the Czechia team rushed out to celebrate.

Ukraine’s week still represented another step forward for a team making its second Billie Jean King Cup Finals appearance. After reaching the semifinals in 2025, Ukraine beat Belgium in the quarterfinals and two-time reigning champion Italy in the semifinals to reach its first final.

content.body:
Karolina Muchova and Linda Noskova led Czechia to a 2-0 sweep of Spain on Friday, sending them into the Billie Jean King Cup final for the first time since 2018.

Muchova, who didn't play in the quarterfinal tie against Great Britain, gave Czechia the early advantage in Shenzhen with a 7-5, 6-4 win over Jessica Bouzas Maneiro in the first match. The hour-long first set was a bit of a slog for the World No. 8, as Bouzas Maneiro had five break points. Muchova fended off four of those, and was more opportunistic in her return games, converting two of her three break-point chances. The second set was more economical for Muchova, who has now won 13 of her last 15 WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz matches dating back to June.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Billie Jean King Cup (@billiejeankingcup)

Following the same script as the quarterfinal tie, captain Barbora Strycova pegged Noskova for the second match, to clinch it. The Wimbledon champion delivered yet again, beating Cristina Bucsa 7-6 (5), 6-2 to send Czechia into the championship tie.

Noskova started strong and finished even stronger against No. 35 Bucsa, winning six of the first seven points in the first set and the final eight points in the second. In between, the World No. 6 escaped a 4-2 deficit in the first-set tiebreaker.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Billie Jean King Cup (@billiejeankingcup)

Czechia -- whose loaded roster also includes Top 30 players Marie Bouzkova and Sara Bejlek, and doubles World No. 1 Katerina Siniakova -- is looking for its 12th Billie Jean King Cup title.

They'll play either two-time defending champion Italy or Ukraine in the championship tie on Sunday.  Italy, which beat home nation China in the quarterfinals, is led by World No. 20 Jasmine Paolini. Ukraine, featuring World No. 7 Elina Svitolina, beat Belgium 2-1 in the quarters. Ukraine's roster initially included fellow Top 10 player Marta Kostyuk, but she pulled out prior to the quarterfinals to rest her wrist.

Italy and Ukraine will play on Saturday, Sept. 26.

content.description: No. 26 seed Emma Navarro upset No. 7 seed Karolina Muchova in the third round of the US Open while No. 21 seed knocked out No. 9 seed Elina Svitolina on a day where No. 6 seed Linda Noskova and No. 11 Marta Kostyuk were also in action and advanced to the round of 16.

content.body:
Five Top 10 players -- and No. 11 Marta Kostyuk -- were all in action at the US Open on Friday, with mixed fortunes. While World No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka and No. 3 seed Jessica Pegula were winning their third-round matches in Arthur Ashe Stadium and Louis Armstrong Stadium, the grounds were also packed with a lot more action.

2024 US Open semifinalist Emma Navarro scored the biggest upset of the Flushing Meadows fortnight so far by beating No. 7 seed Karolina Muchova and No. 21 seed Anna Kalinskaya knocked out No. 9 seed Elina Svitolina while Wimbledon champion and No. 6 seed Linda Noskova - survived a game effort from American No. 29 seed Ann Li.

Here's how it all went down. 

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Kostyuk returns to Round of 16

Kostyuk def. Alexandrova, 6-3, 6-2

How it unfolded: Kostyuk largely had things her own way against Alexandrova, against whom she had previously been 0-2.

She raced out to a 5-1 lead in the first set before eventually securing it, and won six straight games from 2-0 down to reach the US Open fourth round for the second year in a row.

'Over the moon' Navarro scores third Top 10 win of comeback

Navarro def. (7) Muchova 6-3, 7-5

How it unfolded: Navarro won the last three games in each set to beat Muchova in their first career head-to-head meeting, in what marked Muchova's earliest exit at the US Open in four years.

Navarro now owns nine career Top 10 wins, but only two of those have come at the US Open. She also defeated then-defending champion Coco Gauff on her way to the semifinals two years ago, and said she was "over the moon" to score another upset -- this time, against a two-time US Open semifinalist -- in front of her home crowd.

“She’s a great player and has had a great year this year. A lot of really good results. I knew it would be tough today. She has a more unique game style on the WTA tour. Definitely unique matchup. But I enjoyed it. I had fun playing today. I’m looking forward to playing again in a few days.” 

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by WTA (@wta)

Noskova denies determined Li, Court 17 crowd

(6) Noskova def. (29) Li 6-2, 6-7(6), 6-2

How it unfolded: Things were not looking all that complicated for Noskova in her first head-to-head meeting against Li over the first hour or so on Court 17 as she built a 6-2, 3-0 lead.

But as her forehand soon went wayward, it allowed Li the confidence to step into her own to erase what was a double-break advantage. The American, a fourth-round performer in Flushing last year, saved a match point with a forehand winner at 6-5 in the tiebreak, and clocked another on the run to extend the match two points later. But after the first four games of the third set went with serve -- which saw Li erase two break points in her hold for 2-2 -- Noskova won the last four games with key play in the clutch. 

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by US Open (@usopen)

Three of the last four games went to deuce, and Noskova saved a break point to extend her lead to 5-2.

"It was such a tough match from the beginning to the very end. A lot of things happened throughout all the three sets, but I'm glad I pulled out the win," Noskova said afterwards. "I somehow pulled it off, and I'm happy and very relieved."

Through to the Round of 16 in New York for the first time, Noskova will face Kostyuk in a rematch of their Wimbledon semifinal.

Kalinskaya through to US Open fourth round for the first time

(21) Kalinskaya def. (9) Svitolina 6-3, 2-6, 6-3

How it unfolded: After the pair split the first two sets, it was Svitolina who broke first in the deciding set to take a 3-2 lead. However, Kalinskaya won four straight games to close out a 6-3, 2-6, 6-3 victory in 1 hour, 52 minutes.

With the win, the 27-year-old advanced to the round of 16 at the US Open for the first time. She has now reached the second week at all four Grand Slam tournaments, having previously done so at the 2024 Australian Open and Wimbledon and the 2026 French Open.

Anna Kalinskaya is into Round 4 of the US Open for the first time in her career! pic.twitter.com/gjBdZlugc6

— US Open Tennis (@usopen) September 5, 2026

Kalinskaya's three wins in New York mark the first time she has won three matches at a tournament since the French Open. It was also her second victory over Svitolina in six career meetings.

She next faces Navarro, against whom she has won both of their previous meetings, including their round-of-32 clash in Doha earlier this year.

content.body:
NEW YORK -- Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova and runner-up Karolina Muchova both opened their US Open campaigns with straight-sets wins, though they couldn't have been more different.

US Open: Scores | Order of play | Draws

Noskova found herself 5-2 down before reeling off five straight games to close out the first set, saving two set points along the way. She extended the run to 10 consecutive games for a 5-0 lead in the second, ultimately winning 11 of the final 12 games to defeat Katie Volynets 7-5, 6-1 in 1 hour and 37 minutes.

Kicks off her campaign 💪

Linda Noskova finds her rhythm and secures the win in straight sets over Volynets 7-5, 6-1.#USOpen pic.twitter.com/ChhSNiKA4P

— wta (@WTA) August 31, 2026

Muchova, meanwhile, needed only 58 minutes to wrap up a 6-3, 6-0 win over Sinja Kraus on Grandstand earlier in the day. No. 15 seed Diana Shnaider also made quick work of her first-round opponent, defeating Daria Snigur 6-0, 6-4 in 68 minutes, while No. 16 seed Sorana Cirstea -- competing in what is expected to be her final US Open -- beat Julia Grabher 6-3, 6-0 in 1 hour and 29 minutes.

Here are more notable results from a busy Monday at Flushing Meadows.

Zheng rallies to beat tricky teen qualifier

Since returning to action, Zheng Qinwen has shown flashes of her pre-injury form but has lacked consistency. Therefore, it was encouraging to see her earn her fourth straight win on Monday, defeating fellow qualifier Kristina Liutova 4-6, 6-3, 6-1 in 2 hours and 28 minutes. Liutova, 16, entered on a nine-match win streak and had won 21 of her last 22 matches.

Zheng has performed well thus far in New York to advance out of qualifying and into the second round, but whether that level can hold up against higher-ranked opponents remains to be seen. A potential clash with No. 12 seed Belinda Bencic could provide those answers if the Swiss can beat Yulia Putintseva in her opener. 

From qualifying into Round 2 👏

Zheng Qinwen outlasts Liutova, 4-6, 6-3, 6-1!#USOpen pic.twitter.com/tIfthncYCr

— wta (@WTA) August 31, 2026
Stephens turns the tables on Tauson

Sloane Stephens doesn't have anything to prove as a Grand Slam champion and former World No. 3, but she put any doubters on notice with a dominant first-round performance against Clara Tauson. The 2017 US Open champ defeated the Dane 6-4, 6-1 in 1 hour and 16 minutes to earn her first Grand Slam main-draw win since Wimbledon 2024.

It was the best Stephens has looked since her return last September, particularly on serve. She won 79% of her first-serve points and finished with 19 winners to just 10 unforced errors for good measure.

Seeded players continued to roll on Day 2, but a couple were dealt a bad hand in the draw and paid the price. 

Cristina Bucsa won the WTA 500 in Merida in February and made her Top 30 debut in March before injuries derailed her season. She had just two wins in her last 11 matches entering the US Open. Meanwhile, No. 28 seed Sara Bejlek entered fresh off reaching the Cincinnati semifinals behind wins over Karolina Pliskova, Krejcikova, Ekaterina Alexandrova, Aryna Sabalenka and Madison Keys. It didn't matter. Bucsa -- defending fourth-round points -- won 7-5, 4-6, 6-1 in 2 hours and 7 minutes.

Taylor Townsend also reached the fourth round in New York last year before suffering a heartbreaking loss to Barbora Krejecikova -- after holding eight match points -- that dashed her quarterfinal hopes. On Monday, she took the first step toward redemption, upsetting Roland Garros finalist and No. 20 seed Maja Chwalinska 6-2, 6-3 in 1 hour and 19 minutes.

content.title: How Muchova and Mensik went from uncertain entry to US Open champions
content.description: Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik won the US Open mixed doubles title Wednesday, defeating Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli. It capped a run that began with uncertainty about getting into the draw -- and about what they'd wear.

related.label: Muchova, Mensik save match points, join Bencic, Cobolli in US Open mixed doubles final
Serena and Venus Williams awarded US Open wild card in doubles

content.body:
NEW YORK -- There was plenty of uncertainty surrounding Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik's run to the 2026 US Open mixed doubles title, which they clinched with a 6-3, 1-6, [10-6] win over No. 4 seeds Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli on Arthur Ashe Stadium late Wednesday night.

Would Mensik raise his ranking enough to earn them a guaranteed spot? If not, would the Czech duo receive a wild card? And above all, what would they wear if they got in?

In the end, the answers were no, yes and matching pink shirts with maroon shorts -- a look that made them best dressed as well as champions.

"My favorite color right now is pink and maroon, that's for sure," Mensik said in their post-match press conference.

Said Muchova: "I think I [also] have to say that my favorite is maroon. Now that Jakub knows what it means, it's the favorite color for both of us."

The red-adjacent color appreciation is nice, but the trophy -- and the $1 million prize -- likely tops it. And it means even more considering how they won it, playing back-to-back matches with no rest while their finals opponents had nearly two hours to recover.

Back-to-back breakers

Muchova and Mensik narrowly escaped defeat in the semis, saving two match points and surviving a match tiebreak against Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev just to reach the final. That comeback -- and the adrenaline that came with it -- seemed to carry straight into the championship match.

They pressured Bencic and Cobolli early, generating three break points in the second game. They couldn't convert, but broke two games later for 3-1 and served out the set from there.

Bencic and Cobolli recovered quickly, running away with the second set to force a match tiebreak. As it did in the semifinal, Mensik's serve delivered in the biggest moments, and he sealed the title with an ace.

An ace for the title! 🏆 pic.twitter.com/VShvPv8GQj

— US Open Tennis (@usopen) August 27, 2026
Tournament in review

Muchova was determined to make the partnership work.

"I really wanted to play with him," she said. "Obviously the ranking was the deciding point because the cut for these mixed doubles is very high. I put a little pressure on him, but in a fun way. It worked. I'm happy we managed to get in and that we are here now."

On paper, they possessed the tools needed to be a strong team. And they proved it immediately on court, defeating doubles specialists Kristina Mladenovic and Marcelo Arevalo -- owners of 13 combined Grand Slam titles -- in the first round.

It was Mensik's first mixed doubles match since he was at least nine years old, he said.

Muchova finishes it at the net!

She and Mensik are one set away from the final. pic.twitter.com/lYXN6vPCKp

— US Open Tennis (@usopen) August 27, 2026

"It sounds crazy, huh," Mensik said. " My first mixed doubles, 100%-win rate, so I will finish my career, I guess," he added with a smile.

"It was a fun event. We went out there to have some fun, to get a couple matches before the main draw. We actually played pretty well. It was starting to [become] the real deal. Obviously [having] gone this far, both of us are very happy we could lift the trophy."

Across four matches -- including a quarterfinal win over Emma Navarro and Tommy Paul -- they won 85% of their first-serve points. They hit 13 aces between the semis and the final.

Reaching new heights

The accomplishment hasn't fully sunk in for Muchova. But make no mistake: while opinions may be mixed on the new format, it will go down as a first Grand Slam title for both players.

"I think I'm not even realizing it yet. We are both singles players, so that's always in my head," she said. "I'm super happy we managed to win. It was not my expectation. I think we'll celebrate a little bit and have some days off. I'm glad we did this together."

For Muchova, it's the latest highlight in a standout 2026 season. She won her first WTA 1000 title in Doha in February -- her first trophy in seven years -- then added her third WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz title in Bad Homburg in June. She reached her second Grand Slam final at Wimbledon in July, falling to compatriot Linda Noskova in three sets, and now owns a US Open mixed doubles crown.

For Mensik, the title sits alongside his win over Novak Djokovic to claim the 2025 Miami Open title and his 2026 Roland Garros semifinal as the biggest achievements of his young career.

content.description: Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik beat Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev to join Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli in the US Open mixed doubles final, where the winner will receive not only the trophy, but also the $1 million grand prize.

content.body:
NEW YORK -- Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik rallied from 3-0 and 8-5 down -- and saved two match points -- to beat Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev 5-4 (6), 3-5, [11-9] on Wednesday night and reach the US Open mixed doubles final.

They join No. 4 seeds Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli, who continued to show why they were one of the most feared duos in the draw in the first semifinal. The Indian Wells champions advanced with a 4-5 (7), 4-1, [10-5] victory over Elina Svitolina and Gael Monfils.

All-Czech duo powers into final

In doubles, it's important for partners to have strengths that play off one another. On paper, it appeared as if that was true of Muchova and Mensik. On the court, it's been proven. Behind Muchova's craftiness and Mensik's raw power, they were able to raise their level in big moments.

Muchova finishes it at the net!

She and Mensik are one set away from the final. pic.twitter.com/lYXN6vPCKp

— US Open Tennis (@usopen) August 27, 2026

Muchova delivered in the clutch early, with a volley winner to close out the first set after a nail-biting opener. Then, after losing the second from a break up, Mensik's serving made the difference in the match tiebreak. The 20-year-old continued adding to his ace count, none bigger than the one to save a match point and level at 9-9. He followed it with another unreturnable serve to earn match point for he and Muchova.

In all, the Czech duo won the last four points to survive and advance.

Bencic and Cobolli stay perfect

While Bencic and Cobolli dropped their first set of the tournament to start the match, things turned around for them down 1-0 and facing three break points in the second. They saved all three and won the final four games of the set to force a match tiebreak, where they capped their comeback with more impressive displays, particularly from up close.

Stellar self-defense from Cobolli at the net! pic.twitter.com/XlI55YtNA4

— US Open Tennis (@usopen) August 27, 2026

Bencic and Cobolli improved to 7-0 as a pair, having dropped only two sets along the way. They'll have a chance to extend their perfect record and go two-for-two in capturing titles later Wednesday night in the final.

While the tournament has been played with sets to four up to this point, the final will be played with full sets to six. In place of a third set, a 10-point tiebreak will remain if necessary. And when the dust settles, not only will the champions collect some hardware, but they'll also be awarded the $1 million grand prize.

content.title: WTA stars Andreeva, Bencic, Svitolina and Muchova reach US Open mixed doubles semis
content.description: The 2026 US Open Mixed Doubles Championship formally got underway Tuesday in New York, and the stars were out in full force. That remained the case at day's end, as four of the Top 12 players in the WTA Rankings and their partners reached the semifinals.
